summary: Children aged 7–10 learn to evidence (not just assert) which everyday material best suits a use by designing and running a fair test: change one thing (the material), measure one outcome, keep everything else the same, then write a conclusion that cites the data. The central objective is planning, controlling variables, measuring, and reasoning from results — ideally with real materials and measurement — and transferring that fair-test logic to a new property. Interactive simulations and consolidation/assessment tasks are supporting scaffolds around that doing-and-measuring core.
misconceptions: Thinking a test is fair while leaving variables uncontrolled (different sample sizes, different forces), so the comparison is invalid.
Changing more than one thing at once and being unable to attribute the result to the material.
Drawing the conclusion from prior belief or expectation rather than from the data collected.
Confusing a fair test with simply 'trying things out' — no controlled comparison, no measured outcome.
Treating a single trial as certain, with no sense that a result might need repeating or could be unreliable.

activities.title: Run a real fair test: which fabric makes the best raincoat?
steps: Pose a decision-worthy question, e.g. 'Which material — nylon, cotton or paper — makes the best raincoat?'
Set up the comparison yourself: cut same-size squares of each fabric, stretch each over an identical cup or tray.

Before testing, agree out loud what will be measured (how much water soaks through / reaches the tray beneath) and what must stay the same (square size, how it is held, the time, the amount of water).
Pour the SAME measured amount of water (e.g. one level cupful) on each square, catching and measuring what passes through (ml collected).
Record each result in a table so the materials can be compared by number, not by eye.

Write the conclusion with a claim–evidence–reasoning frame, using your own results, e.g. if nylon let the least water through: 'Nylon was the most waterproof material we tested, so it is the best choice for keeping rain out, BECAUSE in our test only 2 ml passed through it, compared with more through the cotton and paper.'
Repeat at least one trial and note any odd result to discuss whether the evidence can be trusted.
activities.insight: A conclusion about a material's use should be earned from a controlled, measured comparison — changing only the material and keeping everything else the same — not asserted from prior belief.

activities.title: Fair-test bench simulation with a fairness check
steps: Choose a question for a test bench, e.g. most waterproof fabric, strongest bag material, or best cup insulator.
Set each variable yourself: deliberately leave sample sizes or amounts uneven first and see what happens.

Watch an optional 'fairness meter' flag the setup red when more than one variable differs, then fix it — lock every sample to the same size and apply the same measured input — and watch it turn green.
Run the test and read the comparable measured result for each material (ml through, mass held before tearing, or °C lost) collected into a table.

Use a sentence builder to complete a claim–evidence–reasoning conclusion from the data, e.g. 'Nylon was the most waterproof BECAUSE only 2 ml passed through it, less than through any other material we tested.'
activities.insight: Controlling variables is what turns a comparison from unfair to trustworthy; only a controlled test yields a clean number you can reason from.

activities.title: Spot the unfair test and sort the variables (consolidation/check)
steps: Decide 'Which test is fair?' between options, including one unfair option where a variable is left uncontrolled, and say what makes the unfair one invalid.
Sort variables into three buckets: the one to change (the material), the one to measure (the outcome), and those to keep the same.
Put the steps of an enquiry into order: question → change one thing → measure → record → conclude from the data.
Match materials to evidence-based uses, justifying each match with a tested property.
activities.insight: Recognising fair vs unfair tests and classifying variables consolidates the structure of a controlled comparison and the habit of concluding from evidence.

activities.title: Label the parts of a fair test (structure reference)
steps: Study an annotated fair-test diagram and identify the changed variable, the controlled variables, and the measured outcome.
Reveal each element's role (why it is changed, controlled, or measured).
Reveal a finished results table and read off how the winning material is identified from the numbers.
activities.insight: A fair test has distinct parts — one changed variable, several controlled variables, and one measured outcome — that together make a comparison trustworthy.

activities.title: A character sets the design brief (optional framing)
steps: Receive a decision-worthy design brief from a character, e.g. 'Help me pick the best material for a lunchbox / umbrella / cup cosy.'
Restate the brief as a testable question and plan what to change, measure, and keep the same before moving to a real or simulated test.
activities.insight: A genuine, purposeful question gives the test a reason to exist and clarifies what counts as 'best'.

checkQuestion: Say: 'You want to find which material makes the best rainy-day coat: cotton, plastic or paper. Set up a test to compare how waterproof they are. Show me how you keep it FAIR, how you'll measure, then tell me which to use and why.' Watch the whole thing, don't coach.
checkAnswer: Pours the SAME amount of water on equal pieces held the same way for the same time, catches/observes what soaks through, and concludes plastic is most waterproof CITING the result ('least water got through') tied to the real use (a raincoat).
